E13 – Op-Amps, Differential Amplifiers and Power Amplifiers (T11, Weeks 9–10)

Source note. There are no lecture slides for Weeks 9–10 (Week 8 ends with “Topics for next week: operational amplifiers”). This pack is written from WS10 (“The basics of operational amplifiers, integrated circuit biasing, differential amplifiers and power amplifiers”, 10 questions, no solutions) and the standard treatment in Boylestad & Nashelsky, Electronic Devices and Circuit Theory (the op-amp chapters and the power-amplifier chapter), which is the textbook the course lists in its references. WS10’s questions are Boylestad end-of-chapter problems, so the notation below is Boylestad’s.

Figures. All values in the WS10 solutions are read from the WS10 PDF figures (Fig. 1–3 on pages 2–3).

Why this matters in the exam: The final is expected to weight Weeks 6–10, and this is the last topic in the course, so it will almost certainly appear. WS10 shows what the course wants you to be able to do: CMRR and output with common-mode error (Q1–Q2), ideal op-amp circuits read off a figure (Q3–Q5), and power-amplifier power and efficiency (Q6–Q10). Every one of these is a short “plug into the right formula” question worth roughly 3–6 marks. They are easy marks if you pick the right formula and do not mix rms and peak values.

1. The core ideas

1.1 Differential and common-mode signals

A differential amplifier (the input stage of every op-amp) has two inputs (non-inverting, +) and (inverting, −).

Common-mode signal What both inputs share (noise, hum); you want it rejected
Output = differential gain, = common-mode gain

1.2 The BJT differential amplifier (DC bias and gain)

Two matched transistors share one emitter resistor (the “tail”) to . Each has its own collector resistor to . Bases at about 0 V DC.

Quantity Formula
Emitter voltage V
Tail current
Each collector current

of each transistor (use the per-transistor current, )
Single-ended output, one input driven

Common-mode gain (single-ended) (with large); small when is large

Why large (or a constant-current source in its place) helps: the tail current then barely changes with a common-mode input, so and CMRR . This is where IC biasing comes in.

IC biasing (current sources), short version. ICs avoid big resistors and capacitors. They replace with a transistor current source:

  • Current mirror: a diode-connected transistor sets a reference current (or when split supplies are used). The matched “mirrors” it: .
  • BJT constant-current source: a divider or Zener fixes . Then , independent of the load. WS10 has no question on these, so expect them only as a short “why” or a one-line current calculation.

1.3 The ideal op-amp: the two rules

  1. No current into either input ().
  2. With negative feedback, (virtual short; is huge, so the difference must be about zero). If is grounded, is a virtual ground (0 V, but no current to ground).

From these two rules you can derive every circuit below. You do not need to memorise them, but in an exam using the result is faster.

Circuit How to recognise it Output
Inverting Input through to the − input; from output to −; + grounded
Non-inverting Input straight into +; from − to ground; from output to −
Unity follower (buffer) Output wired straight to −; input to + (gain 1, very high , very low )
Summing (inverting) Several inputs, each through its own , all to the − input; one
Multi-stage One op-amp output feeds the next input Multiply the stage gains (each stage is ideal, so no loading)

Traps:

  • The non-inverting gain is , not .
  • The sign matters. An inverting stage gives a negative (or 180° shifted) output. For an rms ac input, give the magnitude and say “180° out of phase”, or give the signed value. For dc inputs the sign is the answer.
  • In a summing amp with ac inputs of the same phase, add the terms. The rms values of in-phase sinusoids add directly.
  • A real op-amp cannot output more than its supply (saturation, roughly ). If you get 360 V, say so.

Type C: ideal op-amp circuit from a figure

  1. Find where the input enters: the + pin (non-inverting) or through a resistor to the − pin (inverting).
  2. Is the output wired straight to −? Then it is a follower.
  3. More than one resistor into the − pin? Then it is a summer.
  4. Write the matching formula, put in the values, and keep the sign.
  5. Several stages: work left to right. Each stage’s output is the next stage’s input.
  6. If a configuration is unfamiliar, go back to the two rules: , and KCL at the − node with zero current into the pin.

Given: mV, mV, ; CMRR = (a) 200, (b) . (The PDF prints the inputs in mV.) Find: .

  1. , so V. Split into parts: V and V.

  2. , so V (the common-mode part is only 10.2 mV).

Comment for the exam: a real op-amp would saturate near its supply rail, so hundreds of volts is not physical. In Boylestad’s original version of this problem the inputs are 200 µV and 140 µV. Then the answers are 365.1 mV and 360.01 mV, which are realistic. Answer the question as printed (mV), and add one line noting saturation. The point being tested is the same either way: low CMRR adds about 1.4% error, high CMRR adds almost none.

4. Traps that cost marks

  • Using the sum instead of the average for . .
  • Putting CMRR in dB straight into . Convert with first.
  • Writing the non-inverting gain as . It is .
  • Dropping the minus sign of an inverting or summing stage, or not stating “180° out of phase” for an rms answer.
  • Mixing rms, peak and peak-to-peak in power formulas. .
  • Series-fed class A: forgetting that is fixed by the bias, not by the signal. Changing changes (WS10 Q7).
  • Class A maximum output: assuming the full when the Q-point is not centred. Take the smaller clipping limit.
  • Class B: assuming transistor dissipation is worst at full output. It peaks at . Also, is for both transistors.
  • Transformer: combining parallel speakers as a series sum, or inverting the ratio ( is wrong).

WS10 Q3 (course question). Calculate the output voltage of the circuit of Fig. 1 for an input of 150 mV rms.

Solution

Read the figure: goes straight into the + input (pin 5). A 36 k resistor runs from the − input (pin 4) to ground, and 750 k runs from the output (pin 10) back to −. Supplies are ±9 V (741). So this is a non-inverting amplifier with k and k.

Rail check: the peak is V, which is inside ±9 V, so there is no clipping.

Trap: alone would give 3.125 V. The “1 +” is worth the mark.

WS10 Q4 (course question). Calculate the output voltage for the circuit of Fig. 2 with inputs of mV rms and mV rms.

Solution

Read the figure: through 47 k and through 12 k both go to the − input (pin 4). There is 470 k feedback, and + (pin 5) is grounded. Supplies are ±15 V. This is an inverting summing amplifier.

So the output is 1.183 V rms, 180° out of phase with the (in-phase) inputs. The peak is 1.67 V, well inside ±15 V.

7. Add to your open-book reference sheet

DIFF / CMRR
 Vd = Vi1 - Vi2     Vc = (Vi1 + Vi2)/2     Vo = Ad*Vd + Ac*Vc
 CMRR = Ad/Ac       CMRR(dB) = 20 log10(Ad/Ac)    ratio = 10^(dB/20)
 Vo = Ad*Vd*(1 + Vc/(CMRR*Vd))          (use the ratio, not dB)
 Measure: Ad = Vo/Vd (Vc=0);  Ac = Vo/Vc (inputs tied)
BJT DIFF PAIR
 IE(tail) = (VEE - 0.7)/RE ; IC = IE/2 ; VC = VCC - IC*RC ; re = 26mV/IC
 single-ended Av = RC/(2re) ; double-ended Ad = RC/re ; Ac ~ RC/(2RE)
 Current mirror: IX = (Vsupply - VBE)/RX, I_out ~ IX
IDEAL OP-AMP: no input current; Vplus = Vminus (neg. feedback)
 Inverting  Vo = -(Rf/R1)V1         Non-inv  Vo = (1 + Rf/R1)V1
 Follower   Vo = V1                 Summer   Vo = -Rf*sum(Vk/Rk)
 Cascade: multiply stage gains, keep signs; check |Vo| < rails
POWER: eta = Po(ac)/Pi(dc); PQ = Pi - Po;  P = Irms^2 R = Ip^2 R/2 = Ipp^2 R/8
 Class A series: IB=(VCC-0.7)/RB, ICQ=bIB, VCEQ=VCC-ICQ*RC
   Pi = VCC*ICQ ; Po = Ic(rms)^2*RC ; Ic,pk(max) = min(ICQ, VCC/RC - ICQ)
   centred: Po,max = VCC^2/(8RC), eta max 25%
 Class A transformer: RL' = a^2 RL, a = sqrt(RL'/RL) ; eta max 50%
   Po = (VCEmax-VCEmin)(ICmax-ICmin)/8 ; Pi = VCC*ICQ
 Class B: Ip = VL(p)/RL ; Pi = 2VCC*Ip/pi ; Po = VL(p)^2/(2RL)
   eta = (pi/4)(VL(p)/VCC), max 78.5% ; P2Q = Pi - Po (both), PQ = P2Q/2
   max: Po = VCC^2/(2RL), Pi = 2VCC^2/(pi RL)
   P2Q,max = 2VCC^2/(pi^2 RL) at VL(p) = 0.636 VCC
